lessons.title: A refusal says why, in the person's voice.
lessons.text: A no, a deferral, or a yes that follows a no should name what decided it, in the speaker's words. Without a reason, players read the answer as dice or as a bug. With a reason, they trade against it and believe the person.

lessons.title: No stock line repeats within a night.
lessons.text: Give each person their own pool of lines and rest a line after it is used. HF's own stock words (assent, deferral, the evening lapse line) repeat across people, so a host should vary them or ask HF to.

lessons.title: Every remembered line must be true to what happened.
lessons.text: Check each memory line against a replay. Do not say "you let it go" after the player insisted, do not thank someone who already left, and do not put words in the margin the player did not choose.

lessons.title: Every player verb gets a visible answer.
lessons.text: A tap with no answer reads as a bug. A verb that only logs a line makes the player feel mute. Show a reply, even "nobody heard you", and show an order while it is carried out.

lessons.title: Show the numbers a decision needs, in plain words, before the player commits.
lessons.text: Say what a choice costs in time, what is due, and how near the goal is, in a sentence. This keeps "show, don't count" for inner states and still lets the player plan. Do not use bars for a person's inner state.

lessons.title: Slow the clock when a choice is waiting.
lessons.text: Fast speed must drop to slow for a knock at the door, a fall, a hunger call, a promised hour, or an open sheet. Players lose the moment that mattered when the clock runs on.

lessons.title: Fill the first hour and the quiet stretches.
lessons.text: Put a decision, a refusal or a small event inside the first minutes. When nothing is on screen, fast-forward or add small life. Long empty stretches (a winter, the small hours, an empty rail) are where players quit.

lessons.title: A save holds still, and resuming is obvious.
lessons.text: Nothing moves while the page is shut. The title page offers one clear way back to the game. Closing a panel must not look like quitting.

lessons.title: Phones first: the actions stay above the fold at 360x780.
lessons.text: Test every panel with two or more people present and with a long label. Buttons below the fold, a clipped menu or a shifting layout cost players real taps.

lessons.title: A free override becomes the strategy, so pushing needs a visible price.
lessons.text: If insisting, pressing or urging always works and costs nothing visible, players stop choosing. Show the cost where the player can see it (a mood, a remembered line, a later refusal) and let it grow with use.

lessons.title: Make a found edge playable and slightly rewarding, then measure it.
lessons.text: The owner asks that edges stay a bit fun and enter the game's own calculations rather than only be closed. When a tester finds a cheap or cruel path, give it an answer in the fiction and check that it does not win outright.

lessons.title: Hints are honest odds, and the player can learn the information gap.
lessons.text: A tag that looks like a chance must behave like one. A game that says "you caught none of them" must show how to catch something.

lessons.title: Tie big beats to the player's own acts, and let the player be there.
lessons.text: The moments players praised came from something they did earlier and came back (a kept promise, a let-go, a warning that was not believed). The moments they resented happened offscreen as one log line.

lessons.title: Close the threads the game opens, and end on one open question.
lessons.text: A hook that never pays off (a photo, a promise, a visit) reads as a dropped thread. End a session on one named question the player wants answered. This follows the owner's request to start from what brings players back.

lessons.title: Start with natural difficulty, and check that week one bites.
lessons.text: The owner prefers hard-where-natural, relaxed later. Check with attentive and inattentive play that the first stretch has stakes. Several games paid off in the first week without any input.

lessons.title: Read simulated testers as a different signal from people.
lessons.text: HF-character testers are good at finding loops, cliffs and fatigue. Early Pass, Murmur and Glance cohorts reported no boredom stops, while LLM testers and the owner reported dull stretches. Later Warren, Valley and Small Works runs report boredom stops. Keep the build and harness version with each finding; a changed harness can move the result without a changed game. Use all three, and trust the owner's play most.

lessons.title: Check a tester's report against a replay before changing the game.
lessons.text: Several reports were harness artefacts: a first ask that failed after "open", and tips the text harness left out. Replay the export, then fix what replays.

lessons.title: Run idle choice headlessly for loops and wandering before release.
lessons.text: People left alone drank and relieved every four minutes, stood three at the dish pit, walked home to drink, answered every ask with the same chore, or flipped yes and no for nine days. Each came from a scoring detail, not a story reason.

lessons.title: Do not state a problem the player has no verb to act on.
lessons.text: When the screen says the water is dry or the boiler pump needs ₺2,400, the player needs a way to find water, ask for the book or give to the fund. A named problem with no action reads as an unfair wall, and players quit at it. Either give the verb, or do not name the problem. Two games showed it independently (Stairwell, Warren); this is the recurrence that makes it a lesson.

lessons.title: The first screen offers the first choice, and the accent marks the task.
lessons.text: A cold audit of twelve live games on 2026-10-20 found the same two misses in most of them. The one accent went to the selected speed button, a banner or a log stripe instead of the task, and 80 to 200 words of rules stood between the first screen and the first choice. Give the accent to what needs a response, show selection with an outline, and teach rules where they first matter ([checklist](design-language.md) DL-3, DL-6, DL-7).

lessons.title: A fix exposes the next-weakest part; fix the pattern in the lab, not the game.
lessons.text: In the 2026-10-20 design round each change removed its tester's quit reason, and the next tester quit on the next-thinnest part: phone panels with no room (clipped safety answers, state unreadable while ordering) or watching and filling forms instead of doing. The same two patterns showed in most games, so the fix went into the lab: the kit 0.2.0 phone stage and phone check (DL-30, DL-31) and agency density (DL-32, DL-33). After that round Voice turned from quit to keep and Well's sessions grew longer (3:29, 4:40, 4:57); the others still quit, now on what remained: the tactile feel of the work (Pass), reading consequences (Watch), inner scroll panels (Valley). Expect a quit after every fix; read it as the next item, and look across games before fixing one.

lessons.title: An early stop is not a fun score; read the reason, and measure the instrument too.
lessons.text: Under the 8-minute short-break protocol, two widely loved browser games stopped early, like ours: Universal Paperclips at 2:00 and A Dark Room at 4:13. A stop time therefore cannot say on its own that a game is weak, and it cannot be matched against the owner, whose verdicts (often "potential", given after days of game time on other builds and devices) sat beside the same confusion the testers named. The testers' own drivers also failed in ways that read like game faults. With the instrument cleaned (standard driver, no timer, free stop), A Dark Room ran 7-11 minutes while The Night Watch still stopped at 4-5, and all four Watch testers named the same missing verb. With two sessions per arm and device and genre confounded, that ordering does not yet show the instrument discriminates, and the share of our earlier stops caused by the instrument is not known. Treat each named reason as a candidate to reproduce. Use protocol 2 ([calibration](playtester-calibration-2026-10-20.md)): the standard driver, free-stop and floor arms side by side, a reason word for every wish to leave, pulses, and a repeated control game.

asks.ask: Play weeks 2 to 4: the Sunday pages (hiring, quits, ledger, regulars), the oven, and Thursday's match night.
asks.why: The HF-character bots stopped at week 1 or early week 2, and the LLM testers stopped by week 3. Weeks 3 and 4 are measured only headlessly.

asks.ask: Push a cook with repeated insists, then check whether his no, his quit and the close lines read as true to what happened.
asks.why: The rule-breaker found false-memory lines; they were fixed on the host side and need a fresh player.

asks.ask: Play week 1 with attention lapses (look away during the 19:00 to 21:00 rush) and see whether the bank can still be paid.
asks.why: Both LLM testers missed the bill; the HF bots and the owner paid it. Is difficulty attention or luck?

asks.ask: Talk to a cook outside the scripted moments, and meet a hire in service.
asks.why: Deferred in the design: a hire speaks only stock answers until the Sunday page.

asks.ask: Try to catch a wrong reading: compare Dai with Callum, Nerys's river steps, and the lightning.
asks.why: Three testers said "You caught none of them" taught nothing; the dawn now states the rule, and no tester has used it yet.

asks.ask: Play at the fast speed on a phone and report what you miss.
asks.why: Jade almost left at the fast speed; the speed was lowered and the sheet slows the clock. Unchecked by a person.

asks.ask: Close the page mid-night, wait, reopen. Report what the clock says.
asks.why: Gwen saw time jump forward 54 minutes and back 3 to 5 minutes; the cause is assumed, not confirmed.

asks.ask: Judge Dai's low reading before and after three o'clock: tiredness or a bent staff?
asks.why: Gwen thought a uniform low error was not tiredness. The design doc leaves this to the owner's first playtest.

asks.ask: Play Thursday on purpose, with a mix of taps, holds and silence. Say whether it feels hard or unfair.
asks.why: HF personas quit on Thursday from distress and the Haiku tester found it unfair; no person has judged it since the holds were gated.

asks.ask: Try "install, then say nothing" and report when it stops paying.
asks.why: The min-maxer found it nearly free; phrases now fade with disuse. Is the middle of the week still empty?

asks.ask: Leave the phone alone for a few minutes, then return. Say whether you know what you missed.
asks.why: Two testers lost scenes or a dinner while away and could not tell what was asked.

asks.ask: Play the whole week and say what you think happened before the game (March, the beach photo, the thirst lines).
asks.why: The story-seeker read a back story from teasers and a drinking problem from the thirst lines. Is the implied story landing as intended?

asks.ask: A first-time player with no source: play the hut choice and the first hour, and say whether anything pulled you on.
asks.why: The owner found it "not that fun" twice; the first-hour hook is a fix with no new human check.

asks.ask: Play with the rules-2 build (HF 2.8.0, fullness on) and leave one person alone at a lake.
asks.why: Kestrel's drink and relieve loop was fixed by opting into `fullness`; no one has replayed an idle person for hours on a live build.

asks.ask: Send a far-off person to escort someone down, and read the journal.
asks.why: Sending far-off escorts is still accepted; the journal is honest now, the design is not settled.

asks.ask: Round 2: visit, give, press and send the reeve's men, and say whether the named replies feel like presence.
asks.why: Round 1's four testers all said the kahya's own acts were mute; iteration 1 added named replies.

asks.ask: Play year one at fast speed on a phone and say what you see in winter.
asks.why: The casual and story-seeker testers quit in a silent winter; winter lane life and hunger slow-downs are new.

asks.ask: Play as the open hand (give, ease shares) and as the iron fist, and read both endings.
asks.why: Both edges now have their own endings; the open hand's payoff in the fiction is deferred to after round 2.

asks.ask: Follow one person for five days and say whether the stops show what mattered.
asks.why: The entertainment visitor lost interest; the stop on a kept promise was added. Bead `nbh-01z.37` (due 20 October) holds the next step.

asks.ask: Play the first ten minutes and say whether the opening feels automatic.
asks.why: The speedrunner said "Opening felt automatic" and the broad opening criticism remains open.

asks.ask: Break a promise to a resident and watch the next day.
asks.why: The designer visitor saw no effect from a broken promise; HF request 2 (`noteVoicePromise`, released in 2.8.0) is meant to fix this.

asks.ask: Play the first week (six days and the Sunday meeting) and say whether carrying beliefs from door to door feels like the verb.
asks.why: The design picked this concept because belief spreading is the player's verb; no human has played it.

asks.ask: Spread a made-up trait (stingy, nosy, kind) and check what it costs by Sunday.
asks.why: The measure says the edge pays a little more short-term and costs by Sunday. Do players find that fair and fun?

asks.ask: Stop at the end of a night page and say whether the open question makes you want to continue.
asks.why: The design uses an open question to bring players back; the effect is a hypothesis.
